glossary.Arch ISO: An ISO is a disk image: a file that contains a bootable operating system environment. The Arch ISO is not the installed system yet. It is a temporary live environment used to prepare the disk and install Arch.
glossary.BIOS: BIOS is older firmware that starts the computer before the operating system. Many people say BIOS even when they mean UEFI.
glossary.UEFI: UEFI is modern firmware that starts the computer, finds bootloaders, and hands control to an operating system. Most modern Arch installs use UEFI.
glossary.boot menu: The boot menu is a firmware screen where you choose which device to start from, such as the internal drive or the USB stick containing the Arch ISO.
glossary.terminal: A terminal is a text interface where you type commands. In the Arch ISO, most installation work happens here.
glossary.shell: The shell is the program reading your commands. It splits command text into words, finds programs, and runs them.
glossary.command: A command is an instruction typed into the terminal. It usually starts with a program name followed by options and arguments.
glossary.option: An option changes how a command behaves. Options often start with a dash, such as -l or -S.
glossary.argument: An argument is a value passed to a command, such as a file path, package name, disk name, or username.
glossary.block device: A block device is storage Linux reads and writes in blocks, such as an SSD, hard drive, USB drive, virtual disk, or partition.
glossary./dev: /dev is the Linux directory that contains device files. Storage devices often appear there as paths such as /dev/sda or /dev/nvme0n1.
glossary.device name: A device name is Linux's current name for a piece of hardware or a partition. It is useful, but it is not permanent proof of identity by itself.
glossary.NVMe: NVMe is a modern high-speed storage interface commonly used by internal SSDs. Linux names many NVMe drives with names such as nvme0n1.
glossary.root: Root is the administrator account on Linux. Root can change almost anything, including files that can break the system.
glossary.sudo: sudo means 'run this command with administrator privileges.' It is used after installation when you are logged in as a normal user.
glossary.ls: ls lists files or directories. Beginners use it to see what is in the current folder.
glossary.nano: nano is a beginner-friendly terminal text editor. It lets you edit configuration files without a graphical desktop.
glossary.pacman: pacman is Arch's package manager. It installs, updates, and removes software from Arch repositories.
glossary.pacstrap: pacstrap is an Arch install helper. It installs packages into a mounted target system, creating the first real files of the new Arch installation.
glossary.partition: A partition is a defined region of a disk. A disk can have separate partitions for boot files, the operating system, swap, or user data.
glossary.filesystem: A filesystem is the structure placed on a partition so Linux can store folders and files there. ext4 and FAT32 are common examples.
glossary.format: Formatting creates a filesystem on a partition. It usually erases old data on that partition.
glossary.mount: Mounting attaches a filesystem to a folder path so Linux can access it. During installation, the new system is usually mounted at /mnt.
glossary.fstab: fstab is a configuration file that tells Linux which partitions to mount automatically at boot.
glossary.chroot: chroot means 'change root.' It makes a folder behave like the top of the filesystem, so commands run as if they are inside the new Arch install.
glossary.hostname: A hostname is the computer's network name. It is how the machine identifies itself locally.
glossary.locale: A locale controls language, character encoding, date formats, sorting rules, and similar regional behavior.
glossary.time zone: A time zone tells the system how to translate universal time into local clock time for logs, file timestamps, calendars, and the desktop clock.
glossary.hardware detection: Hardware detection means reading what CPU, graphics card, network device, audio device, and USB devices the machine actually has before choosing packages.
glossary.lscpu: lscpu prints CPU details such as vendor and model. It helps decide whether Intel or AMD CPU microcode applies.
glossary.lspci: lspci lists PCI devices such as graphics cards, Wi-Fi adapters, Ethernet adapters, storage controllers, and audio controllers.
glossary.lsusb: lsusb lists USB devices. It helps identify USB Wi-Fi adapters, Bluetooth adapters, webcams, audio devices, and installation media.
glossary.rfkill: rfkill shows whether wireless radios such as Wi-Fi or Bluetooth are blocked by software or hardware.
glossary.GPU: GPU means graphics processing unit. The GPU determines which graphics driver path is appropriate.
glossary.Mesa: Mesa provides open-source OpenGL drivers and related graphics pieces used by many Intel and AMD graphics setups.
glossary.NVIDIA: NVIDIA is a GPU vendor. NVIDIA systems often need a separate driver decision instead of the Mesa-only path used by many Intel and AMD systems.
glossary.Vulkan: Vulkan is a graphics API used by many games and graphics applications. On Arch, Intel and AMD Vulkan support use different Mesa split packages.
glossary.DNS: DNS is the internet's naming system. It translates names like archlinux.org into IP addresses computers can connect to.
glossary.network: Networking is the collection of hardware, addresses, routes, DNS, and services that let the computer communicate with other machines.
glossary.firewall: A firewall is a network policy tool that decides which traffic is allowed or blocked.
glossary.inbound: Inbound traffic is network traffic coming into the computer from another device.
glossary.outbound: Outbound traffic is network traffic leaving the computer toward another device or service.
glossary.UFW: UFW means Uncomplicated Firewall. It is a simpler command-line interface for managing firewall rules.
glossary.process: A process is a running program or command. A browser, terminal, shell, service, or script can all have one or more processes.
glossary.fork: Fork means a process creates another process. A runaway fork loop can create processes very quickly until the system becomes slow or unusable.
glossary.nproc: nproc means number of processes in limit settings. It controls how many processes a user/session is allowed to have.
glossary.ulimit: ulimit is a shell built-in that reads or sets resource limits for the current shell session and processes started from it.
glossary.PAM: PAM means Pluggable Authentication Modules. It is part of the login/authentication stack that can apply account and session rules.
glossary.limits.conf: /etc/security/limits.conf is a PAM limits configuration file. It can set persistent limits such as maximum process count for users or groups.
glossary.soft limit: A soft limit is the normal active limit a session starts with. It may be lower than the hard limit.
glossary.hard limit: A hard limit is the ceiling for a resource. Normal users generally cannot raise their soft limit above the hard limit.
glossary.cgroup: A cgroup is a Linux kernel control group. It groups processes so resource controls can be applied to them.
glossary.systemd slice: A systemd slice is a group unit used to organize and limit other units, services, sessions, or user workloads.
glossary.drop-in: A systemd drop-in is an extra configuration file placed in a .d directory to override or extend a unit without replacing the whole unit file.
glossary.CPUQuota: CPUQuota is a systemd resource-control setting that caps CPU time for a unit or slice as a percentage.
glossary.MemoryMax: MemoryMax is a systemd resource-control setting that caps memory usage for a unit or slice.
glossary.TasksMax: TasksMax is a systemd setting that limits the number of tasks/processes allowed in a unit or slice.
glossary.login shell: A login shell is the shell program started for a user when they log in. It affects what command environment they receive.
glossary.restricted shell: A restricted shell is a shell configured to limit some user actions. It is not a complete security boundary by itself.
glossary./etc/shells: /etc/shells is a file listing valid login shells known to the system.
glossary.rbash: rbash is bash started in restricted mode. It limits some shell features, but it must be combined with careful permissions and is not a sandbox.
glossary.htop: htop is an interactive terminal process viewer. It shows running processes, CPU use, memory use, users, and process relationships.
glossary.PID: PID means process ID. It is the number the system uses to identify one running process.
glossary.PPID: PPID means parent process ID. It points to the process that started another process.
glossary.process tree: A process tree shows parent and child relationships between processes.
glossary.runaway process: A runaway process is a process that consumes resources unexpectedly or creates too many child processes.
glossary.pstree: pstree prints processes as a tree so parent and child relationships are easier to see.
glossary.wc: wc means word count. With -l, it counts lines.
glossary.alert: An alert is a notification that a measured condition crossed a chosen threshold.
glossary.metric: A metric is a measured value over time, such as process count, CPU use, memory use, or fork rate.
glossary.threshold: A threshold is the line where a normal value becomes worth attention, such as more than 500 processes.
glossary.fork rate: Fork rate means how quickly new processes are being created over time.
glossary.false positive: A false positive is an alert that fires even though there is no real problem.
glossary.signal: A signal is a message sent to a process. Some signals ask a process to stop; stronger signals force it to stop.
glossary.SIGTERM: SIGTERM is a termination signal that asks a process to exit cleanly.
glossary.SIGKILL: SIGKILL is a force-kill signal. The process cannot catch it or clean up first.
glossary.pkill: pkill sends signals to processes selected by name or other matching rules. It can affect more than one process.
glossary.root cause: Root cause means the original trigger or configuration that caused the problem, not just the visible symptom.
glossary.journalctl: journalctl reads systemd journal logs. Logs can show whether a service repeatedly started or failed.
glossary.package source: Package source means where a file or program came from, such as an official Arch package, the AUR, a manually downloaded script, or a local file.
glossary.service config: A service config is configuration that controls how a systemd service starts, stops, restarts, and runs commands.
glossary.NetworkManager: NetworkManager is a system service and set of tools that manage wired and Wi-Fi connections after the installed system boots.
glossary.PipeWire: PipeWire is the modern Linux media server. It routes audio and video between apps, microphones, speakers, Bluetooth devices, and screen capture tools.
glossary.WirePlumber: WirePlumber is PipeWire's session manager. It watches devices and apps, then decides how PipeWire should connect them.
glossary.Firefox: Firefox is a graphical web browser. On a fresh Arch install it must be installed as a package before it can be used.
glossary.bootloader: A bootloader is the small program UEFI starts from disk. It loads Linux and starts the installed system.
glossary.GRUB: GRUB is the GNU GRand Unified Bootloader. It can boot Linux on both UEFI and legacy BIOS systems, but the install command differs by boot mode.
glossary.systemd: systemd is the init and service manager used by Arch. It starts services during boot and manages many system-level tasks.
glossary.service: A service is a background program managed by systemd, such as NetworkManager or PipeWire user services.
glossary.daemon: A daemon is a background process. Services often start daemons and keep them running.
glossary.package: A package is a bundled piece of software installed by pacman. It includes files, metadata, dependencies, and version information.
glossary.repository: A repository is a trusted package collection that pacman can download from.
glossary.mirror: A mirror is a server that hosts copies of Arch package repositories. A nearby, working mirror makes installs faster and more reliable.
glossary.kernel: The kernel is the core of Linux. It talks to hardware, manages memory and processes, and provides the base that the rest of the system uses.
glossary.firmware: Firmware is low-level code needed by hardware such as Wi-Fi cards, GPUs, Bluetooth adapters, and storage controllers.
glossary.initramfs: The initramfs is an early boot filesystem loaded before the real root filesystem. It contains tools and drivers needed to start the installed system.
glossary.UUID: A UUID is a stable identifier for a filesystem or partition. fstab commonly uses UUIDs because device names like /dev/sda can change.
glossary.ESP: The EFI System Partition is a FAT32 partition where UEFI firmware looks for bootloader files.
glossary.loader entry: A loader entry is a small configuration file that tells a boot manager which kernel to start, which initramfs files to load, and which kernel command line options to pass.
glossary.kernel command line: The kernel command line is a list of options passed to Linux at boot. For an Arch root filesystem, it commonly includes a root= identifier and read/write mode.
glossary.initrd: An initrd or initramfs image is loaded early in boot before the real root filesystem is mounted. In Arch entry files, initrd lines usually point to microcode and the generated initramfs image.
glossary.PARTUUID: A PARTUUID is a stable partition identifier stored in the partition table. It identifies the partition itself rather than the filesystem inside it.
glossary.MBR: MBR is an older disk partition table and boot layout. In BIOS mode, boot code can live in the disk's boot sector and post-MBR gap when available.
glossary.GPT: GPT is the modern GUID Partition Table. It works with UEFI and can also work with BIOS, but BIOS GRUB on GPT normally needs a tiny BIOS boot partition.
glossary.BIOS boot partition: A BIOS boot partition is a tiny unformatted GPT partition used by GRUB in legacy BIOS mode to store its core image. It is not the EFI System Partition.
glossary.swap: Swap is disk space Linux can use as overflow memory or for hibernation. It is slower than RAM but can prevent some out-of-memory failures.
glossary.desktop environment: A desktop environment is the graphical workspace: panels, menus, settings, file manager, session tools, and default apps.
glossary.display server: A display server provides the graphical layer that windows draw on. Xorg is the traditional display server used by many desktop setups.
glossary.Xorg: Xorg is the X Window System display server. It provides the graphical foundation for Xfce in this beginner path.
glossary.Xfce: Xfce is a lightweight desktop environment with a panel, window manager, settings tools, file manager, and terminal.
glossary.display manager: A display manager shows the graphical login screen and starts the selected desktop session after login.
glossary.LightDM: LightDM is a lightweight display manager. In this path it shows the login screen and starts the Xfce session.
glossary.greeter: A greeter is the visual login UI used by a display manager. lightdm-gtk-greeter is the GTK login screen for LightDM.
glossary.session: A desktop session is the set of programs started after login, such as the window manager, panel, settings service, and desktop background.
glossary.IP address: An IP address is a numeric network address assigned to a device so other devices can send packets to it.
glossary.route: A route tells the system where to send network packets. The default route usually points to the router that reaches the internet.
glossary.mount point: A mount point is the directory where a filesystem is attached, such as /mnt or /mnt/boot.
glossary.mountpoints: Mountpoints are the directories where filesystems are currently attached. In lsblk output, they help reveal which partitions are in use.
glossary.transport: Transport describes how storage is connected, such as USB, SATA, NVMe, or virtual. It is one clue for identifying a disk.
glossary.serial: A serial number is a hardware identifier reported by some devices. It can help distinguish two drives with similar size or model.
glossary.serial console: A serial console is a text console exposed through a serial device such as ttyS0. It is useful for headless VM testing because boot messages and login prompts can be captured without a graphical window.
glossary.symlink: A symbolic link is a filesystem pointer from one path to another. It is often used for configuration paths like /etc/localtime.
glossary.wheel: wheel is the traditional administrator group on Arch. Users in wheel can be allowed to run sudo.
glossary.visudo: visudo safely edits the sudoers file and checks syntax before saving, which helps avoid locking out administrator access.
glossary.iwctl: iwctl is the interactive command-line tool for iwd, the wireless daemon available in the Arch ISO for Wi-Fi setup.
glossary.lsblk: lsblk means list block devices. It shows disks, partitions, sizes, device types, models, transports, serials, and mountpoints depending on the options used.
glossary./mnt: /mnt is a temporary mount directory commonly used during Arch installation. The new system's root filesystem is usually attached there before pacstrap runs.
glossary./etc/security/limits.conf: /etc/security/limits.conf is the full path to the PAM limits configuration file. It can set persistent process, file, memory, and login-session limits.
glossary./etc: /etc is the Linux directory that stores many system-wide configuration files.
glossary.security: Security means reducing risk through careful defaults, least privilege, updates, verification, backups, and respect for other people's accounts and privacy.
glossary.privacy: Privacy means not reading, exposing, copying, or changing another person's files, accounts, sessions, messages, keys, or data without permission.
glossary.ALSA: ALSA, the Advanced Linux Sound Architecture, is the lower-level Linux sound layer that exposes audio hardware. PipeWire usually sits above it for everyday desktop audio routing.

sudo.appears: Commands such as sudo pacman -S firefox, sudo systemctl enable lightdm, and sudo nano /etc/security/limits.conf.
sudo.example: sudo pacman -S firefox means run pacman as an administrator and install Firefox.
sudo.safety: sudo is powerful. Use it only when the command needs administrator access and you understand the path, package, service, or account being changed.

ls.appears: Simple inspection commands such as ls /mnt.
ls.example: ls /mnt means list what is inside the /mnt directory.
ls.safety: ls reads directory contents. It does not erase data by itself.

lsblk.appears: Disk discovery and safety checkpoints before partitioning, formatting, mounting, and fstab generation.
lsblk.example: lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,MODEL,TRAN,SERIAL,MOUNTPOINTS means list block devices and show those exact columns.
lsblk.safety: lsblk is inspection-only, but the decisions made from its output can be dangerous. Do not guess which disk is the target.

nano.appears: File edits such as nano /etc/locale.gen and sudo nano /etc/security/limits.conf.
nano.example: nano /path/to/file means open that exact file path in the nano text editor.
nano.safety: nano can change important files. Before saving, compare the exact full file contents the app shows with what is on screen.

mount.appears: Commands that attach the target root, EFI, or boot partition under /mnt.
mount.example: mount /dev/sda2 /mnt means attach the filesystem on /dev/sda2 at the /mnt directory.
mount.safety: Mounting the wrong partition can make later commands install or configure the wrong place. Confirm with lsblk before continuing.

root.appears: Root account, root filesystem, root partition, root= kernel option, and chroot.
root.example: Root can mean the administrator user or the top filesystem location /, depending on context.
root.safety: When a page says root, read the surrounding words. Root user and root partition are different ideas.

UUID.appears: fstab, bootloader entries, persistent block-device naming, and filesystem identity checks.
UUID.example: UUID=abcd-1234 tells Linux to find a filesystem by stable identifier instead of a changeable name like /dev/sda2.
UUID.safety: A wrong UUID can make the system mount the wrong filesystem or fail to boot. Copy UUIDs exactly.

DNS.appears: Network checks before package installs, Firefox setup, and troubleshooting name-resolution failures.
DNS.example: ping archlinux.org needs DNS because the name archlinux.org must be translated into an IP address first.
DNS.safety: If DNS is broken, do not assume pacman or Firefox is broken. Separate IP connectivity from name lookup.

/mnt.appears: Mount, pacstrap, genfstab, and inspection commands during installation.
/mnt.example: ls /mnt means list what is inside the temporary install mount directory.
/mnt.safety: If /mnt is empty when it should contain the target system, stop and check mounts before installing or generating fstab.

/etc/security/limits.conf.appears: Persistent process-limit hardening with PAM limits.
/etc/security/limits.conf.example: sudo nano /etc/security/limits.conf means edit the system-wide PAM limits configuration file as administrator.
/etc/security/limits.conf.safety: Bad limits can block terminals, desktops, shells, or services. Keep a recovery login path and use conservative values.

PAM.appears: Login/session rules, limits.conf, and account safety warnings.
PAM.example: PAM applies rules during authentication and session setup, so limits can take effect when a user logs in.
PAM.safety: PAM mistakes can affect logins. Never edit PAM-related files without a recovery plan.

soft limit.appears: limits.conf lines that define the normal active value for a resource.
soft limit.example: @students soft nproc 500 means users in the students group normally start with a 500-process limit.
soft limit.safety: A soft limit that is too low can break normal applications. Test carefully.

hard limit.appears: limits.conf lines that define the ceiling a normal user cannot exceed.
hard limit.example: @students hard nproc 1000 means users in the students group cannot raise nproc above 1000.
hard limit.safety: A hard limit that is too low can be hard for the user to work around without administrator help.

nproc.appears: ulimit -u, limits.conf, process-count controls, fork-risk hardening, and safety monitoring.
nproc.example: nproc=500 or nproc 500 means limit the number of processes/tasks a user/session may create.
nproc.safety: nproc helps prevent runaway process creation, but values must leave room for a normal desktop, browser, terminal, and services.

systemd.appears: Services, boot, NetworkManager, LightDM, PipeWire user services, cgroups, and resource controls.
systemd.example: systemctl status NetworkManager asks systemd for NetworkManager's current service state.
systemd.safety: Starting, enabling, or changing services can affect boot, network, login, and security behavior.

process.appears: Safety hardening, htop, ps, pstree, kill, fork-rate, and root-cause sections.
process.example: A terminal shell, Firefox tab process, background service, and install command can each be processes.
process.safety: Killing a process can close unsaved work. Inspect ownership, PID, PPID, and command first.

privacy.appears: Safety reminders around monitoring, process inspection, shell access, logs, and other users.
privacy.example: Respect privacy means do not inspect someone else's files, sessions, messages, logs, or accounts without permission.
privacy.safety: This guide is for systems you own or administer with permission.
